members.summary: Frozen configuration for every Rectified Flow variant.

parameters.name: sample_size
parameters.description: Spatial resolution of a sample.

parameters.name: in_channels
parameters.description: Channels per sample.

parameters.name: out_channels
parameters.description:
Kept equal to `in_channels`: the field is a velocity in the
sample's own space, so it cannot change the dimension.

parameters.name: act_fn
parameters.description:
Activation inside the velocity field.  The reference
implementation calls this `swish`, which is the same function.

parameters.name: base_channels
parameters.description: Width of the first stage — the reference configs' `nf`.

parameters.name: channel_mult
parameters.description: Per-stage width multipliers; the length sets the ladder depth.

parameters.name: num_res_blocks
parameters.description: Residual blocks per resolution.  Four, not two, on CIFAR-10.

parameters.name: attention_resolutions
parameters.description:
Spatial sizes at which self-attention is applied — one resolution
only, unlike the multi-resolution attention of the U-Net Flow
Matching borrows.

parameters.name: dropout
parameters.description: Dropout inside residual blocks.

parameters.name: resnet_groups
parameters.description:
Upper bound on GroupNorm groups; the actual count is
`min(channels // 4, resnet_groups)`, as in the reference.

parameters.name: fir
parameters.description:
Whether resampling goes through a finite-impulse-response filter
rather than nearest-neighbour / average pooling.  Off at
`32 x 32`, on at `256 x 256`.

parameters.name: fir_kernel
parameters.description: Separable filter taps, normalised to unit sum at build time.

parameters.name: progressive
parameters.description: Whether the output is accumulated through a resolution pyramid.

parameters.name: progressive_input
parameters.description: Whether a downsampled copy of the input is injected at each stage.

parameters.name: embedding_type
parameters.description: Where the time embedding's frequencies come from.

parameters.name: fourier_scale
parameters.description:
Standard deviation of the random frequencies when
`embedding_type="fourier"`.  Ignored otherwise.

parameters.name: skip_rescale
parameters.description:
Divide residual and attention sums by $\sqrt{2}$, keeping
the activation variance from growing with depth.

parameters.name: init_scale
parameters.description:
Gain applied to the last convolution of each block.  Zero makes
every residual branch start as the identity, which is what the
reference configs set.

parameters.name: scale_by_sigma
parameters.description:
Divide the network output by the conditioning value `t * 999`.
All four released 256x256 configs set this; the CIFAR-10 one does
not, hence the default.  It is part of the trained function, so a
checkpoint and its flag have to agree.

parameters.name: t_schedule
parameters.description:
Which times the objective draws.  `"uniform"` is the
rectified-flow / reflow objective; the others pin `t` and turn
the same loss into k-step distillation.

parameters.name: time_eps
parameters.description:
Lower end of the time interval.  Times are drawn from
`[time_eps, 1]` and solves run over the same range, matching the
reference implementation.

parameters.name: solver
parameters.description:
Method handed to `lucid.diffeq.odeint`.  `dopri5` is the
embedded Runge–Kutta 4(5) pair the reference calls `rk45`.

parameters.name: rtol
parameters.description: Solver tolerances — the reference's `ode_tol`.

parameters.name: atol
parameters.description: Solver tolerances — the reference's `ode_tol`.

parameters.name: trace_method
parameters.description:
How the divergence is obtained when scoring likelihood.  `None`
picks by dimension.  Irrelevant to training.

parameters.name: trace_noise
parameters.description: Probe distribution for the Hutchinson estimate.

parameters.name: exact_trace_max_dim
parameters.description:
Dimension below which `trace_method=None` resolves to
`"exact"`.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import RectifiedFlowConfig
>>> RectifiedFlowConfig().t_schedule
'uniform'
>>> RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=32, in_channels=3).data_dim
3072
>>> RectifiedFlowConfig(t_schedule=4).is_distillation
True
notes:
`in_channels` and `out_channels` must agree: the field lives in
the sample's own space.

members.summary: Rectified Flow with the training loss, reflow and `.generate()`.
members.extended:
`forward(x)` returns a `DiffusionModelOutput` whose `loss`
is eq. (1).  `forward(x, noise=...)` is the reflow objective over a
previous flow's couplings, which `reflow_pairs` produces.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Architecture, schedule and solver settings.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowForImageGeneration,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowForImageGeneration(cfg).eval()
>>> model(lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))).loss.shape
()
>>> model.generate(n_samples=2, steps=1).samples.shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
notes:
Reference: Liu, Gong, and Liu, *"Flow Straight and Fast"*, ICLR, 2023
([arXiv:2209.03003](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03003)).  Reported: a one-step FID of **4.85** on CIFAR-10,
state of the art among one-step diffusion and flow models at
publication.

A full run is three stages, all through this one class:

1. train with `forward(x)` — the 1-rectified flow;
2. `reflow_pairs()`, then train with `forward(z1, noise=z0)`;
3. optionally rebuild with `t_schedule="t0"` and train on the same
   pairs — one-step distillation.

attributes.name: rectified_flow
attributes.description: Underlying velocity field, exposing straightness and likelihood.

members.name: RectifiedFlowModel

methods.name: input_dim
methods.summary: int: Flattened width `D` of one sample.

methods.name: t_schedule
methods.summary: str or int: Which times the objective draws.

methods.name: trace_method
methods.summary: str: How the divergence is obtained when scoring likelihood.

methods.name: nfe
methods.summary: int: Field evaluations spent by the most recent solve.
methods.extended:
A training step solves nothing and leaves the count where the last
solve put it.  The number the paper is about: a straight flow needs
one.

methods.name: sample_times
methods.signature: sample_times(batch: int, device: str | None = None)
methods.summary: Draw the times the objective is evaluated at.
methods.extended:
Four behaviours, one per `t_schedule`:

* `"uniform"` — $t \sim U[\varepsilon, 1]$, the objective
  itself and what reflow retrains under.
* `"t0"` — every `t` at $\varepsilon$.  Regressing there
  makes one Euler step a generator: one-step distillation.
* `"t1"` — every `t` at 1, distilling the reverse map.
* `k` — the `k`-point grid a `k`-step Euler sampler visits,
  for `k`-step distillation.

parameters.name: batch
parameters.description: How many times to draw.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Where to allocate them.  Defaults to the device the model's
parameters are on; an explicit value wins.

examples:
>>> import dataclasses
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> t = model.sample_times(6)
>>> t.shape
(6,)
>>> bool(((t >= cfg.time_eps) & (t <= 1.0)).all().item())
True
>>> # k = 2: only the two times a two-step Euler sampler visits.
>>> two_step = RectifiedFlowModel(dataclasses.replace(cfg, t_schedule=2))
>>> sorted({round(v, 4) for v in two_step.sample_times(64).tolist()})
[0.001, 0.5005]

methods.name: path_sample
methods.signature: path_sample(x1: Tensor, x0: Tensor, t: Tensor)
methods.summary: The point $x_t = t x_1 + (1 - t) x_0$ on the straight line.

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` data samples.

parameters.name: x0
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` samples from the source distribution.

returns.description:
`(B, C, H, W)` interpolation.  This is Flow Matching's
optimal-transport path at $\sigma_{\min} = 0$.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x1, x0 = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)), lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.tensor([0.25, 0.75])).shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.zeros(2)), x0))
True
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.ones(2)), x1))
True
>>> half = model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.full((2,), 0.5))
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(half, (x0 + x1) / 2))  # the chord's midpoint
True

methods.name: conditional_target
methods.signature: conditional_target(x1: Tensor, x0: Tensor, t: Tensor)
methods.summary: The velocity of that line, $x_1 - x_0$.
methods.extended:
Independent of `t` — a straight line traversed at constant speed
has one velocity — which is why `t` is accepted but unused.  It
stays in the signature because the quantity *is* a function of
time in general, and a caller comparing paths should not have to
special-case this one.

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` endpoint samples.

parameters.name: x0
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` endpoint samples.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: `(B,)` times, accepted for interface symmetry.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x1, x0 = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)), lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> target = model.conditional_target(x1, x0, lucid.tensor([0.2, 0.7]))
>>> target.shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
>>> chord = (model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.ones(2))
...          - model.path_sample(x1, x0, lucid.zeros(2)))
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(target, chord))  # one velocity for the whole line
True

methods.name: rectified_flow_loss
methods.signature: rectified_flow_loss(x1: Tensor, noise: Tensor | None = None)
methods.summary: One optimisation step of eq. (1) — no ODE is solved.

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description:
`(B, C, H, W)` targets.  Data for the first flow; the
*previous flow's samples* during reflow.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description:
`(B, C, H, W)` sources.  Omitted, they are drawn
independently and this is the 1-rectified flow.  Supplied as
the noise that *produced* `x1`, the very same call becomes
the reflow objective — the pairing is the whole difference.

raises.description:
If the model is configured to distil but no pairing is given.
Distillation regresses at a fixed time, which is only
meaningful against the coupling a previous flow produced;
independent draws there would train the field to predict the
mean of the data, and would do so silently.

examples:
>>> import dataclasses
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x1, z0 = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)), lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> loss, prediction, target = model.rectified_flow_loss(x1, noise=z0)
>>> loss.shape, prediction.shape
((), (2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(target, x1 - z0))  # the pairing sets the target
True
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(loss, ((prediction - target) ** 2).mean()))
True
>>> distil = RectifiedFlowModel(dataclasses.replace(cfg, t_schedule="t0"))
>>> distil.rectified_flow_loss(x1)  # a pinned time needs paired noise
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: t_schedule='t0' pins the time, ...

methods.name: sample
methods.signature: sample(n_samples: int = 1, steps: int | None = None, device: str | None = None, noise: Tensor | None = None)
methods.summary: Generate by integrating the field from noise to data.

parameters.name: n_samples
parameters.description: How many samples to draw.  Ignored when `noise` is given.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description:
Force a fixed-budget Euler solve with this many uniform steps.
**This is the setting the method exists for**: a straight flow
is integrated exactly by Euler, so quality at `steps=1`
measures straightness directly.  Left `None`, an adaptive
solve runs instead and spends whatever the tolerance demands.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Where to allocate the prior draw.  Defaults to the device the
model's parameters are on; an explicit value wins.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description:
`(N, C, H, W)` starting point in place of a fresh draw.
Keeping it is what makes a reflow pair.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> model.sample(n_samples=2, steps=1).shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
>>> model.nfe  # steps=1: a single field evaluation
1
>>> noise = lucid.randn((3, 3, 8, 8))
>>> model.sample(noise=noise, steps=4).shape  # the batch follows noise
(3, 3, 8, 8)
>>> model.nfe  # Euler, so the budget is exactly the step count
4
notes:
Euler is used for the fixed-budget path rather than a higher-order
method on purpose: the paper's claim is about the error a *single
first-order step* makes, and a Runge–Kutta step would hide it by
spending four evaluations per step.

methods.name: reflow_pairs
methods.signature: reflow_pairs(n_samples: int = 1, steps: int | None = None, device: str | None = None, noise: Tensor | None = None)
methods.summary: Couplings $(Z_0, Z_1)$ for the next rectified flow.
methods.extended:
Draws from the source, solves the current flow forward, and
returns both ends.  Theorem 3.3 is what licenses feeding these
back in: the solve preserves the marginals, so `z1` is still
distributed as the data while the pair is no longer independent —
and it is that dependence the next round exploits.

parameters.name: n_samples
parameters.description: How many pairs to generate.  Ignored when `noise` is given.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description: Fixed Euler budget instead of an adaptive solve.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Where to allocate the prior draw.  Defaults to the device the
model's parameters are on; an explicit value wins.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description: Sources to use in place of a fresh draw.

returns.description:
`(z0, z1)`, both `(N, C, H, W)` — pass them straight to
`rectified_flow_loss(z1, noise=z0)`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> noise = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> z0, z1 = model.reflow_pairs(noise=noise, steps=2)
>>> z0 is noise, z1.shape
(True, (2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(z1, model.sample(noise=z0, steps=2)))  # z0's endpoint
True
>>> _, _, target = model.rectified_flow_loss(z1, noise=z0)
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(target, z1 - z0))  # the next round's target
True
notes:
This is the expensive half of the method.  The paper generates on
the order of a million pairs before each reflow round, and it is
the only place a solve appears in training at all.

methods.name: one_step
methods.summary: The one-step map $z_0 + v(z_0, \varepsilon)$.
methods.extended:
A single explicit Euler step across the whole interval.  Exact if
the flow is straight, which is what reflow and then `t0`
distillation are for; on a 1-rectified flow it is a crude
approximation and is expected to look it.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description: `(N, C, H, W)` source samples.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> import lucid.nn as nn
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> # The output layer starts near zero; give it weights so the check bites.
>>> _ = nn.init.normal_(model.field.conv_out.weight, std=0.05)
>>> noise = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> out = model.one_step(noise)
>>> out.shape, model.nfe
((2, 3, 8, 8), 1)
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(out, model.sample(noise=noise, steps=1)))
True

methods.name: straightness
methods.signature: straightness(noise: Tensor | None = None, n_samples: int = 1, steps: int = 32, device: str | None = None)
methods.summary: The measure $S(\mathbf{Z})$ of paper eq. (3).
methods.extended:
$$
S(\mathbf{Z}) = \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}\Bigl[
    \bigl\| (Z_1 - Z_0) - \dot{Z}_t \bigr\|^2
\Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Estimated by stepping the flow on a uniform grid, recording the
field along the way, and comparing each velocity against the chord
the trajectory actually spans.  Zero exactly when every path is a
straight line at constant speed — and therefore exactly when one
Euler step is enough.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description:
`(N, C, H, W)` starting points.  Fixing them is the only way
to compare two models fairly, since the measure is an
expectation over the source.

parameters.name: n_samples
parameters.description: How many paths to average over when `noise` is not given.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description: Grid resolution for both the solve and the quadrature.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Where to draw the paths when `noise` is not given.  Defaults
to the device the model's parameters are on; an explicit value
wins.

returns.description: Scalar estimate, in the sample's own squared units.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> import lucid.nn as nn
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> noise = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> s = model.straightness(noise, steps=4)
>>> s.shape, model.nfe
((), 4)
>>> bool(s.item() < 1e-8)  # a fresh field barely moves, so nothing bends
True
>>> _ = nn.init.normal_(model.field.conv_out.weight, std=0.05)
>>> bool(model.straightness(noise, steps=4).item() > 0.0)
True
notes:
Reported per-dimension (a mean, not a sum), so the number is
comparable across resolutions.

methods.name: log_prob
methods.summary: Per-sample $\log p_1(x)$ in nats.
methods.extended:
Integrates the field from `t = 1` back to `t = time_eps`
alongside the accumulated divergence, then scores the arrival
against the standard normal the path starts from.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` data samples.

examples:
>>> import math
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x = lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8))
>>> log_p = model.log_prob(x)
>>> log_p.shape
(2,)
>>> # A fresh field is effectively zero, so x is scored as N(0, I) itself.
>>> const = 0.5 * model.input_dim * math.log(2 * math.pi)
>>> gauss = -0.5 * (x.reshape(2, -1) ** 2).sum(dim=-1) - const
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(log_p, gauss, atol=1e-2))
True
notes:
With `trace_method` resolving to `"hutchinson"` — which it does
at any image size — this is an unbiased *estimate*, and two calls
on the same input will not agree.

The flow is only a normalizing flow while `t_schedule` is
`"uniform"`.  A distilled model is trained to be stepped a fixed
number of times, not integrated, so its density is not the one it
generates from; this method does not refuse it, but the number
means less than it appears to.

methods.name: forward
methods.summary: Evaluate the velocity field at `(x, t)`.

members.summary: Velocity field trained to transport along straight paths.
members.extended:
`forward(sample, t)` evaluates $v(x, t; \theta)$.  Everything
that makes it the paper's method is separate, and each piece maps onto
one part of it:

* `path_sample` — the straight line $t x_1 + (1-t) x_0$.
* `conditional_target` — its velocity, $x_1 - x_0$.
* `rectified_flow_loss` — the objective, eq. (1).  With a
  `noise` argument it is the reflow objective; with a pinned
  `t_schedule` it is distillation.
* `sample` — integrate $t: \varepsilon \to 1$.
* `reflow_pairs` — generate the `(z0, z1)` couplings the next
  round trains on.
* `straightness` — the measure $S(\mathbf{Z})$ that reflow
  is supposed to reduce.
* `one_step` — $z_0 + v(z_0, 0)$, exact once the flow is
  straight.
* `log_prob` / `bits_per_dim` — integrate back, tracking
  the divergence.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Architecture, schedule and solver settings.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.rectified_flow import (
...     RectifiedFlowConfig, RectifiedFlowModel,
... )
>>> cfg = RectifiedFlowConfig(sample_size=8, base_channels=16,
...                           channel_mult=(1, 2), num_res_blocks=1,
...                           attention_resolutions=())
>>> model = RectifiedFlowModel(cfg).eval()
>>> loss, _, _ = model.rectified_flow_loss(lucid.randn((2, 3, 8, 8)))
>>> loss.shape
()
>>> model.sample(n_samples=2, steps=4).shape
(2, 3, 8, 8)
notes:
Reference: Liu, Gong, and Liu, *"Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to
Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow"*, ICLR, 2023
([arXiv:2209.03003](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03003)).  Eq. (1) is the objective, eq. (3) the straightness
measure, and Theorem 3.3 the marginal preservation that makes reflow
legitimate.

**On the coupling.**  `rectified_flow_loss(x1)` draws `x0`
independently, which is the 1-rectified flow of the paper.  Passing
`noise=` supplies a *paired* `x0` instead and is what turns the
same call into reflow — there is no separate objective.

**On transfer.**  Nothing here requires the source to be Gaussian.
The paper's other half — transporting between two image domains
rather than from noise — is the same objective with `x0` drawn from
the first domain instead of a prior, so it goes through
`rectified_flow_loss`, `sample` and `reflow_pairs`
unchanged by passing `noise=`.  Only `log_prob` assumes a
standard normal at `t = 0`, and a likelihood is not defined for a
domain-to-domain transport anyway.

**Where to run it.**  Training is a plain convolutional forward and
backward with no solve, so it belongs on `"metal"`.  Generating
reflow pairs is a solve per batch and is the expensive part of the
method; the paper generates on the order of a million.

**Not implemented, and why.**  Two settings the reference exposes are
absent rather than overlooked:

* **A perceptual reflow loss.**  The reference offers `lpips` and
  `lpips+l2` alongside `l2` for the distillation stage.  Both
  score images through a pre-trained external network, which Lucid's
  compute paths may not depend on, so only the squared error is
  available here.  It is the reference's own default.
* **The stochastic sampler.**  The reference can add noise of
  magnitude `(1 - t) * sigma_variance` to turn the probability-flow
  ODE into an SDE.  Its default is `0`, and the paper is stated and
  evaluated as an ODE method, so sampling here is deterministic given
  the starting point.

Weight averaging (the reference's `ema_rate`) is a property of a
training loop rather than of a model, and is not part of any family
in this zoo.

summary: Rectified Flow family — Liu, Gong & Liu, 2023 (straight paths, reflow).
citation: Liu, Xingchao, Chengyue Gong, and Qiang Liu. "Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow." International Conference on Learning Representations, 2023.
theory:
Given any coupling of two distributions — in the generative case
$X_0 \sim \pi_0$ noise and $X_1 \sim \pi_1$ data, drawn
independently — the **rectified flow** induced by that pair is the ODE



$$
\mathrm{d}Z_t = v(Z_t, t)\,\mathrm{d}t, \qquad Z_0 \sim \pi_0,
$$

whose field is fitted along the straight line between the endpoints,



$$
\min_v \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}\Bigl[
    \bigl\| (X_1 - X_0) - v(X_t, t) \bigr\|^2
\Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t,
\qquad X_t = t X_1 + (1 - t) X_0 .
$$

This is the paper's eq. (1), and its minimiser is the conditional
expectation $v^X(x, t) = \mathbb{E}[X_1 - X_0 \mid X_t = x]$.

**Relation to what came before.**  The objective is exactly Flow
Matching's optimal-transport path at $\sigma_{\min} = 0$: the
interpolation is the same, and the regression target
$X_1 - X_0$ is the same and equally independent of $t$.
What Rectified Flow adds is not a different loss but what is done
*with* the trained model.

**Marginal preservation (Theorem 3.3).**  The solve is not merely a
sampler that happens to work — $\mathrm{Law}(Z_t) = \mathrm{Law}(X_t)$ at every $t$, so $Z_1$ is distributed
as the data while $(Z_0, Z_1)$ is a *different*, non-independent
coupling of the same two marginals.  That is what makes the next step
legitimate.

**Reflow.**  Because the endpoints of the solve are themselves a valid
coupling, the whole procedure can be applied to its own output:



$$
\mathbf{Z}^{k+1} = \mathtt{RectFlow}\bigl((Z_0^k, Z_1^k)\bigr),
\qquad (Z_0^0, Z_1^0) = (X_0, X_1).
$$

Each round trains on the *previous* model's (noise, sample) pairs
instead of independent draws.  The marginals never move — every
$\mathbf{Z}^k$ generates the same data distribution — but the
transport cost never increases and the paths get straighter.

**Straightness** is what improves, and it is measurable:



$$
S(\mathbf{Z}) = \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}\Bigl[
    \bigl\| (Z_1 - Z_0) - \dot{Z}_t \bigr\|^2
\Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t ,
$$

zero exactly when every trajectory is a straight line traversed at
constant speed.  A straight flow is one the forward Euler method
integrates **without discretisation error**, so $S \to 0$ is
precisely the statement that one step suffices — which is why the
paper reports a state-of-the-art one-step FID of 4.85 on CIFAR-10.

**Distillation** is the same loss with $t$ pinned rather than
drawn: regressing $v(\cdot, 0)$ onto $Z_1 - Z_0$ over the
reflow pairs makes $z_0 + v(z_0, 0)$ a direct one-step map.
Reflow is what makes that regression easy — it is fitting an already
nearly-straight path, not shortcutting a curved one.

Time runs from noise to data: $t = 0$ is $\pi_0$ and
$t = 1$ is $\pi_1$.
